Commentary.Commentary: The umpires and the players are out in the middle. Mitchell Marsh and Travis Head walk in with their blades for Australia. Matt Henry has the new ball in hand and is raring to go. Let's play...
Welcome back for the run chase!
…THE RUN CHASE…

With 182 runs needed for victory, the stage is set for an exciting chase. Can Australia kick off the series with a win, or will New Zealand’s bowlers rise to the occasion and defend this total? Stay tuned as we’ll be back shortly with the second innings.

Tim Robinson is in for a chat. He says that the ball was swinging and the surface was greasy. He and Daryl Mitchell worked together to navigate the tough period, and although they had some chances, Robinson was satisfied with the outcome.

Australia started strongly with the ball, striking early to claim three quick wickets. However, they lost momentum during the middle overs, struggling to make further inroads.Ben Dwarshuis was the standout with two wickets, while Josh Hazlewood and Matthew Short picked up one each. Adam Zampa kept things tight with a tidy spell, though he went wicketless. Australia were let down by a couple of dropped catches in the outfield, missed chances that could prove costly if the chase doesn't go their way.

New Zealand have posted a competitive total of 181/6 in their 20 overs, thanks to a brilliant unbeaten century from Tim Robinson. After being put in to bat, the Kiwis found themselves in deep trouble at 6/3 in the second over, but a crucial 92-run partnership between Robinson and Daryl Mitchell steadied the innings. Mitchell contributed a handy 34, while Bevon Jacobs, though struggling for fluency, provided valuable support. The standout performer, however, was Robinson, who anchored the innings superbly. He remained unbeaten on 106 off just 66 deliveries, including five towering sixes, guiding New Zealand past the 180-mark and into a strong position.

OUT! RUN-OUT! Outstanding fielding in the deep sends Bevon Jacobs packing! A yorker on leg stump is squeezed out by Tim Robinson, who makes room and guides it toward deep backward point. Marcus Stoinis puts in a superb effort on the boundary, diving to keep the ball in play and flicking it brilliantly to Travis Head. Head fires in a sharp throw to the keeper, Alex Carey, who collects it cleanly and whips off the bails in a flash. Bevon Jacobs, stretching to complete the third run, puts in a desperate slide, but his bat bounces just as it crosses the crease. The third umpire takes a look, and the big screen flashes OUT! Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS! At the halfway mark, New Zealand are well placed at 93/3. After an early stumble with three quick wickets, Tim Robinson and Daryl Mitchell have steadied the ship impressively. Their partnership has laid a solid platform, and New Zealand will now be aiming for a total in excess of 190. Australia, on the other hand, began strongly but have come under pressure since the powerplay. They'll be eager to break this partnership and halt the scoring momentum to regain control of the innings.

Commentary.Commentary: Done with the pre-match formalities. All in readiness for the action to commence. Tim Seifert and Devon Conway to open the innings for New Zealand. It will be Josh Hazlewood with the ball for Australia. Let's play...

It's very windy and cold at Bay Oval, but at least it's dry and no rain is expected tonight. The teams and match officials get a traditional welcome on the field as they line up for the national anthems. We start with the anthem of Australia, followed by that of New Zealand. Live action is coming shortly.
In tribute to Gordon Carey, the father of Alex Carey, who passed away last week following a long battle with leukemia, the Australian team will wear black armbands.

Michael Bracwell, the New Zealand skipper, says that he is not unhappy with batting first as the teams batting initially have done well here. Adds that they want to put a good score on the board. Shares that Ben Sears, Ish Sodhi, and James Neesham are missing out of the XI today.

Mitchell Marsh, the Australian skipper, wins the toss and opts to bowl. Says that the stats indicate bowling first. Adds that they want to have a look at the wicket first and mentions that they have five changes from their last team.
Australia (Playing XI) - Travis Head, Mitchell Marsh(C), Matthew Short, Tim David, Alex Carey(WK), Marcus Stoinis, Mitchell Owen, Ben Dwarshuis, Xavier Bartlett, Adam Zampa, Josh Hazlewood.
New Zealand (Playing XI) - Tim Seifert(WK), Devon Conway, Tim Robinson, Daryl Mitchell, Mark Chapman, Bevon Jacobs, Michael Bracewell(C), Zakary Foulkes, Kyle Jamieson, Matt Henry, Jacob Duffy.
TOSS UPDATE - Australia have won the toss and opted to BOWL.

So, who will strike first in this high-octane series? Will it be the Men in Yellow or the Black Caps? Stay tuned as we bring you the toss and team news shortly. This is a contest you won’t want to miss!

Australia, meanwhile, enters the series riding high on recent T20I series wins against West Indies and South Africa. With Mitchell Marsh at the helm, the Aussies bring a dynamic, aggressive style of play. Their batting line-up features heavy hitters like Tim David, Travis Head, and Mitchell Owen, while the bowling unit includes the experienced Josh Hazlewood, Adam Zampa, Ben Dwarshuis, and rising star Xavier Bartlett. Matthew Short and Marcus Stoinis return to the squad and will be looking to make an immediate impact, especially with Glenn Maxwell sidelined due to injury. Given their recent form and squad depth, the Men in Yellow will fancy their chances against the hosts.

New Zealand, however, are without several of their first-choice players in Mitchell Santner, Lockie Ferguson, Glenn Phillips, and Finn Allen, all miss out. Stepping up to lead the side is Michael Bracewell, who will rely on the experienced batting core of Devon Conway, Tim Seifert, Mark Chapman, and Daryl Mitchell. In the bowling department, Matt Henry will spearhead the attack, supported by Kyle Jamieson, Jacob Duffy, Ben Sears, and Ish Sodhi. The Black Caps suffered a late setback with Rachin Ravindra ruled out due to a facial injury, prompting a call-up for James Neesham. Despite the absentees, the Kiwis boast a strong, well-rounded squad and will be eager to kick off their home season with a win.

Hello, and a warm welcome to our coverage of the Chappell-Hadlee T20I Trophy, 2025. The Trans-Tasman rivals—Australia and New Zealand—are set to clash in a three-match T20I series, unfolding at the stunning Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui. With three games packed into just four days, the schedule may be intense, but it offers both sides a golden opportunity to fine-tune their squads ahead of the T20 World Cup early next year.
…MATCHDAY…

When neighbours collide, sparks fly higher than the fences! And here we are, at the start of something short, sharp, but oh-so-sweet - the CHAPPELL-HADLEE T20I Trophy! Three matches, four days, two rivals who share more than just a Tasman Sea. This series can be seen as preparation for the upcoming 2026 T20I World Cup. For Australia, it’s a fine-tuning exercise, while it’s the beginning of a long home summer for New Zealand, where England and the West Indies will follow later this year. And for us? It’s popcorn time! Australia walk into Mount Maunganui for the first T20I with the swagger of a team that always finds a way to reload. Mitchell Marsh leads them, but there’s no Pat Cummins, no Mitchell Starc, no Glenn Maxwell, no Nathan Ellis, no Josh Inglis. Sounds like a half-empty jug? Not really! Because in walk Travis Head, Marcus Stoinis, Tim David, and Adam Zampa - the usual suspects who can flip a game on its head. Depth, power, and intent - three words that define this Aussie squad. But what about their concerns? Let’s not ignore them. Josh Inglis’ calf injury has left the wicketkeeper’s gloves in Alex Carey’s hands. Carey’s T20I record isn’t jaw-dropping, but he brings maturity and calmness. Then there’s the question of bowling firepower. Josh Hazlewood is the old, trusted metronome, but with Starc retired and Ellis away, can the likes of Xavier Bartlett, Ben Dwarshuis and Sean Abbott handle the heat? Australia want answers, and this series might just provide them. And then there’s Marcus Stoinis - a man with both muscle and motivation. After missing a few series for franchise cricket, he’s back. This is his chance to shout loud - ‘Pick me for the next T20I World Cup!’ Alongside him, Matthew Short, returning from injury, has a golden opportunity to cement his place. For Stoinis and Short, these three matches aren’t just T20Is, as they’re auditions. Now swing the spotlight to the Kiwis. Oh boy, are they stretched thin! No Kane Williamson, no Mitchell Santner, no Lockie Ferguson, no Finn Allen, no Glenn Phillips. It feels like half the first-choice squad is sitting at home or in recovery. However, New Zealand’s strength has never been in big names - instead, it has always been in its fighting spirit. Michael Bracewell steps in as captain, cool-headed, steady with the bat, and someone who knows how to marshal troops. He’s reliable. And maybe, just maybe, reliability is what they need against the Aussies’ chaos. Devon Conway becomes the anchor in Williamson’s absence. Classy, stylish, calm, and he is the batting heartbeat of this side. If Conway fires, New Zealand can stand tall. Alongside him, Rachin Ravindra, the new face of Kiwi hope, has the chance to step up and shine. Ravindra has shown glimpses of stardom already, and this is the stage where he can prove he belongs at the very top of world T20 cricket. Bowling? Here’s where New Zealand’s story gets fascinating. Kyle Jamieson returns, a giant of a man, literally and figuratively, with bounce that can rattle even the most settled batter. Ben Sears, back from injury, adds raw pace and energy. Add Ish Sodhi, the leggie who has troubled Aussies before, and with Santner missing, expect him to bowl in crunch overs against Australia’s power hitters. So, you get a bowling lineup that might look thin on paper but still has the tools to sting. Always remember, never underestimate a Kiwi bowler with the ball in hand at home. And now, let’s imagine the duels! Travis Head vs Kyle Jamieson - will the pull shot win against bounce, or will Jamieson’s height prove too hot to handle? Tim David vs Ish Sodhi - chaos versus calm, entertainment versus calculation. Marcus Stoinis vs Ben Sears - muscle versus raw pace, the ultimate clash of intent. And flip it the other way - Devon Conway vs Hazlewood - timing vs accuracy, a duel of patience, Ravindra vs Zampa - young brilliance vs spin wizardry, and Bracewell vs Marsh - captain vs captain, brains vs brute force. Oh, the drama that awaits! The stage itself adds more flavour. Bay Oval might be a batter-friendly deck. Flat track, short boundaries, and a sea breeze that teases captains during field placements. High scores are the norm here, and with both teams stacked with six-hitters, don’t be surprised if 200 feels just about par. The crowd? Expect a carnival. Families, flags, drums, and chants that will echo through Mount Maunganui. Head-to-head numbers tell their own story, as Australia lead 13-6 in 19 matches. The last time these two sides met in T20Is? A clean sweep by Australia, in New Zealand’s own backyard. Painful memories for the Black Caps, motivating ones for the Aussies. Will history repeat, or will the Kiwis write a new script? So, here we are - Australia with depth, power, and auditioning stars, while New Zealand have fight, heart, and home advantage with them. Both with questions to answer, both with pride to protect. One thing is certain - Mount Maunganui won’t stay quiet. Buckle up, because this trans-Tasman rivalry will explode!
